output:
# Glenmore, and what happens next

I have been putting off writing this, which is part of how I have made such a bad job of telling people in the first place. Some of you heard about the sale before I had told you properly, and others have had pieces of it over the phone, without the whole picture. That is my fault. I do not want it going around the family in bits any longer, with one person hearing one version and somebody else filling in the gaps, so I am going to set it all down here as honestly as I can.

The house at Glenmore is sold, subject to the usual closing business. I agreed the sale on 3 November, and it is due to close on 15 January 2027. I know that will be a shock to some of you, even if you have already heard it. Seeing a date attached to it makes it different, and I am sorry that the date has reached some of you second-hand.

I am not writing this to make everyone agree with me, or to persuade you that I have done everything right. I have not. I should have spoken to people sooner, and Declan in particular. But I do want you to understand why I made the decision, what sort of place Glenmore has been for us, and what is not being sold or thrown away with it.

The house is near Oughterard, as you all know: the old Mulkerrin place, built in 1931 by Tom’s grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin. Tom grew up there. However many years I lived with him, and however well I know every room and every awkward door, I have always understood that the house held a whole life before I ever came into it. There are marks and stories in it that belong to people none of the younger cousins ever met. It is not simply a building that belonged to Tom and me, and it would be foolish of me to write as though I were the only person with a claim on its meaning.

My own life is in it too. Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind the house in 1979. It was raining, of course, and the cattle were standing there watching us. There was nothing especially grand about it, except to the two of us. Whenever I went out the back afterwards, even to do something completely ordinary, there was often some small part of me that remembered that evening.

The children learned to swim in the lake below the house. Declan used to refuse to come out until his lips were blue, and no amount of telling him that he must be frozen made any difference. Those are not the sort of memories that become less real because the house passes to somebody else. Still, I know that a place can hold memories in a way nothing else quite does. You can turn a corner or put your hand on a wall and be back forty years without warning. I am not going to insult anyone by saying that none of that matters, or that a few photographs will do just as well.

Since Tom died in March 2024, I have been driving out to Glenmore every fortnight. It is about forty minutes each way. I air the house, check the pipes, look for whatever has gone wrong since the last visit, and try to make sure that an empty house does not become a neglected one. At first I did it because it needed doing and because I could not bear the thought of letting the place go. Later, I think I was also doing it because I did not know what else to do. If I kept going out and checking on things, I could keep the question of the house at a distance for another fortnight.

I want to be honest about something I have not told any of you until now. Last February, I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I fell hard and I could not get myself up straight away. I lay there for about twenty minutes before I managed it. There was nobody in the house and nobody within calling distance.

I was not badly injured, which is probably why I found it easy enough to say nothing afterwards. I did not want a fuss, and I did not want everyone immediately telling me that I must never go out there alone again. More than that, I did not want to admit to myself what the fall had shown me. I had been managing by not thinking too far ahead. Afterwards, that became harder to do.

Since then, I have been afraid of being alone at the house. Not every minute, and not in some dramatic way, but enough that the drive out and the walk around it have changed. I listen to the weather differently. I look at a wet step or a dark afternoon differently. A place where I once pottered around without a thought has begun to ask more of me than I can safely give it. I am seventy-one. I cannot keep maintaining it from a distance, and I cannot pretend that another winter or two will somehow make that easier.

There were practical matters too. I had Ó Flaithearta’s do a roof survey in September. Their estimate for the slates and the back chimney came to €38,000. That did not include everything connected with the damp in the back bedroom. The septic tank needs replacing as well, and that would have to be dealt with in order to sell the house to anyone anyway.

I am not putting those figures here as though the whole decision can be settled by a repair estimate. They are not a moral argument, and they do not answer anyone’s grief. Even if the money for the roof had been sitting in an account, I would still have had to face the fact that the house needs steady attention and occupation, not a widow driving out every second week to open windows and wonder what the next winter will bring. But the repairs are part of the truth, and you are entitled to hear them rather than being told vaguely that the place had become “too much”.

Over the best part of two years, I have slowly come to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house. I did not arrive at that thought all at once. For a long time, selling Glenmore felt like a second loss that I was being asked to choose for myself. There are still days when it feels like that. There is also some relief now that a decision has been made, and I have felt guilty about the relief. I would rather say that plainly than make myself sound completely serene about something that has often made me miserable.

Tom used to say that the house should have children in it, not be a museum. He did not say it as an instruction for what I was to do after his death, and I am not going to turn it into one now. He said it because he believed a house was for living in: noise in the rooms, boots at the door, somebody lighting a fire because they were actually cold, not because visitors were coming to look at the old place. His words matter to me, but they do not make this painless, and they cannot be used to tell anyone else that they ought to feel fine about the sale.

There was more than one offer. The price I have agreed is fair, but it is lower than what the Dublin crowd offered during the summer. I took the lower offer on purpose. That is not because there was anything wrong with the other people for offering more, nor because money has ceased to matter to me. It was because of who Aoife and Kevin Joyce are and what they want the house for.

Kevin is from Maam Cross. They are a young couple with two small children, and they want to live at Glenmore. They are not buying it to turn it into a holiday let. They know it is an old house and that it needs work. When I think of Tom saying that it should have children in it, that is the part of the sale that gives me some consolation.

I know perfectly well that “a nice young family are buying it” does not resolve everything. It would be a poor sort of comfort if I used it to close down every difficult feeling. Their children will make their own lives there, not recreate ours. Rooms will change. The place will not be preserved as we remember it. But it will be warmed and used and argued in and laughed in, and I would rather that than watch it slowly decline while I pay visits to keep the damp at bay.

The Joyces have also said that family will be welcome to come out and walk the land any time. That was kindness on their part, and I appreciate it. I know it is not the same as having your own key and being able to walk into the house without asking anyone. I will not pretend otherwise.

Now I have to say something to Declan directly, though the rest of you may as well hear it too, because this is part of what happened.

Declan found out about the sale from his cousin Gráinne on WhatsApp, not from me. That was not Gráinne’s fault. He should have heard it from his mother. He rang me at two in the morning his time, and he said I was “selling Dad”.

It was an ugly conversation. I was hurt by those words, and instead of hearing the grief underneath them, I became angry. I said things back that I should not have said. I am sorry for that. I cannot now present myself as the calm, reasonable person in the story when I was nothing of the sort on that phone call.

I regret not consulting Declan before I agreed the sale. He deserved to hear what I was facing at the house and what I was considering, and he deserved a proper opportunity to speak to me about it. At the same time, I was not willing to put everything off until his visit next summer. I know those two statements may sound as though I am trying to apologise and defend myself in the same breath. Perhaps I am. But both are true. I should have involved him sooner, and I still reached the point where I could not wait until summer before making a decision about my own safety and the continuing upkeep of the place.

Declan, I am not angry with you. You do not have to ring me and say that you understand, and you do not have to approve of the sale. I would rather an honest conversation than a polite one in which we both pretend nothing happened. If you want to write instead, do that. If you need a little time before doing either, I will have to accept that. My door is open, and I hope we can find our way back to talking without either of us reaching for the cruellest thing available.

To the rest of you as well: I am sorry for how you found out. I should have made the phone calls, however difficult they were going to be. Instead, I kept telling myself that I would explain everything properly when the whole matter was settled, as if there would be a moment when it would become easy. There was never going to be such a moment. I am not apologising for the decision itself, because I believe I have made the right decision for me and for the house. But the way some of you learned of it was wrong, and I own that.

As for what is staying with the family, the dresser is going to Úna’s. Pádraig’s fiddle is being kept. So are the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign. They are not compensation for losing the house, and I am not going to describe them as though objects can neatly replace a place. They matter because of what they are and who handled them. The fiddle was played by hands we can still picture. The photographs hold faces that might otherwise drift into being only names. The lamp and the sign are ordinary things in one sense, but ordinary things are often the ones that catch you unexpectedly.

We will sort through the rest carefully before the house is cleared. I do not want that to happen in a rush at the end, with people discovering afterwards that something they loved has disappeared. If there is a particular photograph you remember, or a story connected with something in the house, tell me. I cannot promise that every request can be met, but I can promise not to treat the clearing as though it were only a practical job to be got through.

Before any of that, I would like us to have a day out at Glenmore together. I am asking everyone who can to come to the house on Sunday, 13 December. We will have soup and sandwiches, and time to walk around the place and the land. Bring wellies. It is still December in Galway, whatever fine notions we may have about strolling down to the lake.

There will be no formal ceremony unless people want to say something themselves. You can come and look into rooms you have not seen in years, walk down to the water, tell stories, take photographs, or stand outside without saying very much. If you are sad, come sad. If you are cross with me, you are still welcome. I would not want anyone to stay away because they felt they had to put on a cheerful face for my benefit.

I know that “anyone who can” is doing a lot of work in that invitation. Úna set up this blog years ago so that the cousins in Boston and Perth and Leeds could keep up with us, and a Sunday gathering in Glenmore is not equally possible for people scattered that far around the world. Nobody is expected to make an unreasonable journey or spend money they have not got. For those who cannot come, I would still love to hear the memory you would most want us to carry into the house that day. Some of the stories may have to be told twice: once there, and once again to you afterwards.

There are people in this family who knew Glenmore before I did, people who spent childhood summers there, and children and grandchildren for whom it has mostly been a place visited rather than a home. Each of those connections is real, and they are not all the same. I cannot decide from Galway what the house ought to mean to each of you. I can only tell you what it has meant to me, and why I have reached the point where love for it is not enough to make me able to care for it.

I do not want my last visits there to be nothing more than regret. Glenmore was built by Pádraig Mulkerrin in 1931, and it has already held several lives. Tom grew up in it. He asked me to marry him in the rain behind it. Our children came out of that lake blue-lipped and stubborn. There were griefs there as well as happiness, and plenty of completely unremarkable days that nobody thought to record. Selling the house does not make any of those things less true.

Neither does keeping every memory require me to keep driving out alone to check the pipes. That sentence has taken me nearly two years to be able to say without immediately arguing with myself.

So, to be completely clear, and so that nobody has to learn the practical facts from somebody else: the sale to Aoife and Kevin Joyce was agreed on 3 November, and completion is due on 15 January 2027. The family day at the house will be on Sunday, 13 December, before it is cleared. There will be soup and sandwiches; bring wellies if you are coming. The dresser, the fiddle, the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign are being kept, with the dresser going to Úna’s. The Joyces intend to make Glenmore their home, and they have said the family may come out and walk the land.

You do not have to reply to this with your blessing. I would rather you said honestly what you feel than that everyone rushed to reassure me. I am sorry for the silence, the delays and the second-hand news. I am not sorry for wanting to live without being frightened on a frosted step, nor for deciding that I cannot carry the house any longer.

Glenmore will not be mine for much longer. Tom is still mine to remember, and yours too, though none of us owns another person’s memory. The house will have children in it again. I take comfort from that, even on the days when the comfort is mixed with a fair amount of pain.

And Declan, whenever you are ready, I am here.
